At the edge of the town, where the houses gave up pretending they belonged to one another, there was a clock tower that had stopped at 4:17.

Nobody remembered when it stopped.

Old Mrs. Vale, who ran the bakery with its blue-painted windows, said it had stopped on the day the sea came into the streets and carried off three bicycles, a doghouse, and the mayor’s hat. The librarian said it had stopped much earlier, during the war, when the town had gone dark and every citizen had been instructed to hang black curtains over their windows. A man named Peter, who repaired radios and had never once been known to exaggerate, claimed the clock had never worked at all.

Still, everyone in town knew it was 4:17 whenever they looked up.

The clock tower stood beside the old station, though trains no longer came there. Grass grew between the tracks. Sparrows nested in the ticket office. A red timetable, faded nearly white by salt wind, listed destinations that no longer existed: Northgate, Bellweather, Saint Orin, The Capital.

The Capital remained, presumably, but nobody in town had been there for years.

At the foot of the tower lived a man named Elias, who kept a shop full of clocks.

There were clocks in the window, clocks on the walls, clocks in drawers, clocks dismantled across his workbench like sleeping insects. Tall grandfather clocks breathed heavily in the corners. Tiny silver watches lay in velvet trays. Brass alarm clocks rang at unexpected hours, as if startled by their own dreams.

Elias repaired them all.

He repaired kitchen clocks that had fallen into soup. He repaired pocket watches recovered from wells. He repaired a cuckoo clock that had been struck by lightning and thereafter announced the hour by screaming.

But he would not repair the clock tower.

“Why not?” children asked, pressing their noses against the glass door of his shop.

“Because it has chosen its time,” Elias said.

This seemed to the children like nonsense, but they enjoyed it. Children enjoy nonsense when it is spoken solemnly.

Every afternoon at 4:17, the town changed slightly.

The baker’s oven gave a low, hollow sigh. The gulls flew inland instead of out toward the water. The schoolteacher forgot the next word in whatever sentence she was saying. The old station bell, cracked and mute, trembled once in its iron frame.

Then the moment passed.

Some people believed 4:17 was a door.

They believed that if you stood beneath the tower at exactly that moment, holding your breath, you might hear someone on the other side. Not ghosts, exactly. Not the dead. Something stranger: the lives you might have lived if you had turned left instead of right, said yes instead of no, boarded a train instead of staying behind.

No one admitted to trying.

Everyone had tried.

Elias tried every day for forty years.

When he was young, he had been in love with a woman named Mara. She had dark hair and a laugh that seemed to arrive before she did. She painted signs for shops, though she secretly wanted to paint ships, storms, distant cities beneath moons of impossible colors.

“You should go,” Elias had told her once.

They had been sitting on the seawall, their shoes dangling over black water. A freight ship moved along the horizon, lit like a floating village.

“Go where?” Mara asked.

“Anywhere.”

She leaned against him. “Would you come?”

Elias had wanted to say yes.

He had imagined trains, hotels, foreign streets, small rooms with open windows. He imagined Mara painting the names of cafés in languages neither of them understood. He imagined himself repairing clocks in places where no one knew his name.

But his father had recently died, leaving him the shop. His mother was ill. The tower clock had begun losing minutes. There were practical matters. Necessary matters. The world, Elias believed then, was built from things that needed tending.

“I can’t,” he said.

Mara was quiet for a long time.

Then she said, “No. I suppose you can’t.”

She left the following spring.

Not dramatically. No slammed doors, no letters thrown into the sea. She bought a ticket at the station and carried one suitcase. Elias stood on the platform beside her while rain tapped at the roof above them.

“What time is it?” she asked.

He looked at his pocket watch.

“Four seventeen,” he said.

The train arrived.

For years afterward, Elias told himself that was why the tower had stopped.

Not because of war, flood, rust, or lightning.

Because the town had held its breath at the exact moment Mara stepped onto a train and disappeared.

Elias never heard from her again.

He repaired clocks. He cared for his mother until she died. He watched the station empty. He watched the town become smaller, quieter, older. People brought him broken things, and he made them move again.

Yet every afternoon, he stood beneath the tower at 4:17.

At first he listened for Mara.

Later, he listened for the version of himself who had gone with her.

He imagined that other Elias: sun-browned, careless, living above a café in some city far from the sea. Perhaps that Elias had children. Perhaps he had become a terrible painter. Perhaps he had died young in a country whose name Elias could not pronounce.

Perhaps he, too, stood beneath some clock tower every day, wondering about the life he had not lived.

One winter morning, long after the bakery had passed to Mrs. Vale’s granddaughter and Peter the radio repairman had gone deaf, a girl came into Elias’s shop.

She was twelve or thirteen, with a yellow raincoat and a bicycle helmet under one arm.

“My watch is broken,” she said.

Elias took it from her. It was cheap plastic, bright pink, scratched at the corners.

“It can be repaired,” he said.

“Everything can be repaired, can’t it?”

He looked at her.

Outside, rain slid down the windows. The clocks ticked in their many competing rhythms.

“No,” he said gently. “But more things than people think.”

The girl watched him work. She did not ask questions. She only stood beside the bench, serious as a doctor.

When he handed the watch back, it read 4:16.

“That’s not right,” she said.

“Give it a moment.”

They waited.

The second hand moved. The minute changed.

4:17.

Above them, from the direction of the tower, came a sound like a deep breath.

Then, impossibly, a bell rang.

Once.

Across the town, doors opened. The baker came out with flour on her hands. The librarian stood in the street. Sparrows burst from the station roof in a gray cloud.

Elias stepped outside.

The clock tower, dark for longer than anyone could remember, showed 4:18.

The girl smiled.

“Did you fix it?” she asked.

Elias looked at the tower, then at the long, grass-filled railway tracks running toward the horizon.

“No,” he said.

And for the first time in forty years, he believed it.
